$L_1$ joins two points on the curve, so its gradient gives an average rate of change.

$L_2$ has the curve's gradient at $P$, so its gradient gives the instantaneous rate $f'(3)$.

methods.description: Distinguish a secant's average rate from the tangent's instantaneous rate at the specified point.

methods.description: Read two convenient points on the tangent and divide the signed change in ordinate by the change in abscissa; round an estimate when requested. Positive, negative, zero and fractional values use the same method.

examples.derivation: For the plotted curve y=0.25x²+0.5, the marked points (1,0.75), (4,4.5) and P(3,2.75) lie on the curve. L1 has equation y=1.25x−0.5 and joins the first two points. L2 has equation y=1.5x−1.75; subtracting it from the curve gives 0.25(x−3)², confirming tangency at P. Therefore L2 gives f′(3). This matches the source's secant/tangent comparison.

The orange line is y=8−4x/3, passing through (1.5,6), (3,4) and (4.5,2). The curve differs from this line by 0.25(x−3)², confirming tangency at P. Its gradient is (2−6)/(4.5−1.5)=−4/3≈−1.33. The grid steps match x=10mm and y=8mm. Reading annotations appear only in the solution. The aligned calculation retains its left-hand side and needs no phantom equals gutter.

The plotted temperature is 1+3.5exp(−0.7t), decreasing towards the horizontal room-temperature line T=1. Independently checking its tangent slopes gives −2.45exp(−0.7t), which remains negative and approaches zero. Both solution tangents use the correct point heights and slopes at t=0.8 and t=3.8. The qualitative answer correctly describes slower cooling and adapts the source's contextual tangent interpretation without requiring algebraic differentiation from the learner.

For y=0.3x²+0.5, P=(1,0.8), Q=(3,3.2) and Q1=(1.5,1.175). The original secant gradient is 1.2; the closer secant gradient is 0.75. The tangent at P has gradient 0.6 and equation y=0.6x+0.2, matching the orange segment. More generally, the secant gradient from x=1 to x=1+h is 0.6+0.3h, approaching 0.6 as nonzero h approaches zero. The answer follows the source's closer-point method.
